prose_unit: Recent local case counts provide a strong baseline for dengue forecasting, while useful cross-district signals may arrive with a delay. We propose LEG-SEIR, a compact lagged-exposure graph--SEIR forecaster. A learned sparse graph and recipient-specific lag weights jointly inform a local-preserving neural branch and imported pressure in a conservative SEIR-inspired decoder. A historical-to-simulated pressure transition connects observed reports to compartment rollout, and horizon-specific mixing combines persistence, local, graph and mechanistic forecasts. We evaluate the model using source-audited Sri Lankan district reports, development-only learning-rate selection and five-seed retrospective testing on 2026 observations. LEG-SEIR achieves mean count RMSE of 79.63, compared with 87.38 for persistence, 81.39 for an identity MLP and 80.76 for a competitive shared-adapter control. Removing the graph or replacing the mechanistic branch increases mean RMSE to 84.16 and 81.26. The improvement is strongest beyond the first horizon. These findings support the complete architecture on this sample, but do not isolate each coupling mechanism or establish prospective generalization. Frozen notebooks, source ledgers, predictions and checkpoints support independent verification.

prose_unit: Dengue forecasts should be evaluated against simple surveillance-based alternatives~\cite{johansson2016evaluation,johansson2019challenge}. Sri Lanka has experienced substantial dengue outbreaks~\cite{tissera2020severe}, and forecasting challenges emphasize comparable evaluation of epidemic predictions~\cite{johansson2019challenge}. At district level, a simple forecast repeats the latest reported count. This persistence baseline requires no training. In our matched evaluation, it achieves RMSE 87.38; several simple controls improve on it (Table~\ref{tab:main}). The research question is whether a coupled spatial--mechanistic model can improve further without losing those competitive local predictors.

prose_unit: Lagged neighbourhood signals have motivated spatial epidemic forecasting~\cite{liucao2026,epignn2022}. We hypothesize that preserving a local predictor while selectively incorporating historical spatial information can improve this task. A compartment decoder also requires an explicit rule for transitioning from observed history to simulated states. These are design motivations tested through forecasting comparisons, rather than established transmission mechanisms.

prose_unit: We investigate this design question through \emph{Lagged-Exposure Graph--SEIR} (LEG-SEIR). A compact shared multilayer perceptron (MLP) models local histories. A learned directed graph and recipient-specific lag weights reuse historical information in two paths: neural graph messages and imported pressure inside an SEIR-inspired rollout. A decaying historical anchor transitions to pressure from simulated neighbour states. A learned horizon-specific mixture retains persistence alongside local, graph and mechanistic outputs.

prose_unit: \textbf{Spatial and local predictors.} Graph WaveNet and MTGNN learn spatial dependencies~\cite{wu2019graphwavenet,mtgnn2020}. Our static sparse receiver/sender graph follows this broad adaptive-graph approach. STID demonstrates strong MLP forecasting with spatial/temporal identity~\cite{stid2022}, while simple linear models can rival complex time-series architectures~\cite{zeng2023nlinear}. These findings motivate local controls; their original tasks are not dengue comparisons.

prose_unit: \textbf{Hybrid epidemic models.} IeRNN combines epidemic recursion and neural neighbouring effects~\cite{iernn2020}; CausalGNN couples graph learning with epidemic equations~\cite{causalgnn2022}. STAN and MPSTAN incorporate transmission-domain knowledge~\cite{stan2020,mpstan2023}. MepoGNN shares a learned graph across neural and metapopulation modules and weights mobility history~\cite{mepognn2023}. HeatGNN models mechanistic heterogeneity~\cite{heatgnn2024}, and M-Graphormer combines spatiotemporal learning with infectious-disease dynamics~\cite{mgraphormer2025}. Thus neither graph--compartment coupling nor historical weighting alone is new.

prose_unit: \textbf{Dengue and lagged influence.} Liu and Cao include lagged neighbourhood memory in multi-disease forecasting~\cite{liucao2026}. Weng et al. study Sri Lankan dengue graph forecasting with environmental inputs~\cite{weng2024graph}; Liu et al. develop an explainable covariate compartmental model for Sri Lankan dengue~\cite{liu2025seirlstm}. Their tasks and inputs differ from our case-only comparison. Our proposed contribution is the specified reuse of recipient-specific case-lag weights in neural messages and imported pressure, with a historical-to-simulated pressure transition and horizon mixing. prose_unit: The evidence supports a compact coupled forecaster on this retrospective sample. The scientific motivation is to use historical spatial information without replacing the local predictor, then transition that information into simulated pressure for longer horizons. Lower error than the identity MLP and matched removals is consistent with that motivation, but it does not identify the cause of improvement. Shared graph modelling, lagged neighbourhood influence and mechanistic neural forecasts all have precedents; the proposed contribution is their specified coupling, not those ingredients individually.

prose_unit: Several limits remain. First, only one country and 18 overlapping final origins are scored, and 2026 motivated earlier design choices. Second, immutable report-release vintages were not recovered, so source reconstruction is retrospective. Third, the experiment did not evaluate the alternative printed-repeat reporting policy. Fourth, the SEIR constants and seven-day solver mapping are assumptions requiring sensitivity analysis; the human-only decoder omits explicit dengue vector dynamics. Fifth, graph removal does not isolate imported pressure, and externally published hybrid models have not been rerun as matched competitors.

prose_unit: Graph foundations include GCN and GAT~\cite{kipf2017gcn,velickovic2018gat}, while DCRNN uses directed diffusion in traffic forecasting~\cite{li2018dcrnn}. Earlier architecture investigations considered traffic encoders ASTGCN and A3T-GCN~\cite{guo2019astgcn,bai2021a3tgcn}, adaptive action-recognition graph encoders~\cite{shi2019aagcn,shi2020msaagcn}, LSTM~\cite{hochreiter1997lstm} and temporal convolutional networks~\cite{bai2018tcn}. These publications establish their original model designs, not accuracy of adaptations to this dataset. STID and N-BEATS support investigating compact identity-conditioned and MLP-based forecasting designs~\cite{stid2022,nbeats2020}. GLNN studies distillation from graph models to MLPs~\cite{glnn2022}; it does not establish that the reverse direction improves epidemic forecasts. RevIN addresses distribution shift through reversible instance normalization~\cite{revin2022}, and GRU-D incorporates missingness and elapsed time in clinical series~\cite{grud2018}. Neither technique is used in the evaluated LEG-SEIR configuration.

Our horizon weights are fixed learned parameters, not the input-conditioned attention of the Transformer~\cite{transformer2017}. These citations describe conceptual context rather than an assertion that our implementation reproduces those architectures.
